name: Ciudad Universitaria front
text: In mid-November 1936 Nationalist columns under Varela and Asensio, spearheaded by Moroccan Regulares and the Legion, crossed the Manzanares and broke into the half-built University City. The XI and XII International Brigades and the anarchist Durruti column fought them building by building: the School of Architecture fell first, the Hospital Clínico became a Nationalist bastion, the Faculty of Philosophy a Republican strongpoint. Durruti was mortally wounded here on 19–20 November. The line then froze for over two years, with sniping, shelling and mine warfare under the faculties, until Madrid surrendered on 28 March 1939. The salient marks the closest Franco's army came to taking the capital by storm.
look: A modern campus rebuilt after the war; a few façades show repaired damage, and a memorial to the International Brigades (2011) stands on the campus. The Hospital Clínico San Carlos occupies the building fought over in 1936.
plan: Best walked from Metro Ciudad Universitaria or Moncloa, combined with the Parque del Oeste bunkers and Casa de Velázquez (about 2–3 hours on foot). Campus buildings are working faculties; view from outside.
disputed: How Durruti was shot (enemy sniper, accidental discharge, or killed by his own side) remains debated.

name: Alcázar of Toledo & Army Museum
text: When the coup failed in Toledo, Colonel José Moscardó shut himself in the Alcázar with Civil Guards, cadets, Falangists and their families, plus a number of left-wing hostages. Republican militias besieged the fortress for 70 days, shelling and mining it until the east side collapsed. On 27 September Varela's Army of Africa relieved it, after Franco had diverted his march on Madrid to do so; the capture of Toledo was followed by killings in the town, including of wounded militiamen in the hospital. The siege became the founding legend of Francoism and the Alcázar was rebuilt as a shrine. Since 2010 it houses the Museo del Ejército.
look: The rebuilt Alcázar, with the Army Museum's Spanish military history galleries; Moscardó's office is preserved and scale models show the fortress before and after the siege.
plan: Museo del Ejército opens Tuesday–Sunday (closed Mondays); allow at least 2 hours. Paid entry, with free periods; check the museum site before travelling.
disputed: The famous telephone call in which Moscardó told his son Luis to 'die like a hero' is questioned by historians: some say Luis was shot about a month later, in reprisal for an air raid, not in response to the call. The fate of the hostages inside is also unclear.

name: Suicide Hill (Colina del Suicidio), Jarama
text: On 12 February 1937, in the Nationalist offensive to cut the Madrid–Valencia road, the British Battalion of the XV International Brigade was thrown onto this knoll above the Jarama valley. For about seven hours it held against Moroccan Regulares and Legionaries supported by artillery and machine guns. Of roughly 600 men who went into action, only a fraction were still standing at nightfall; the writer Christopher Caudwell was among the dead. Neighbouring Dimitrov and Franco-Belgian battalions suffered similarly. The line bent but held, and the Jarama front froze here until 1939.
look: An open, olive-and-scrub hilltop with an informal stone cairn and plaques; traces of trenches and scattered shrapnel remain in the fields around.
plan: Morata de Tajuña publishes nine waymarked battle routes; route 7 starts here. Park carefully on the M-302 tracks; no facilities, bring water in summer.
disputed: Casualty figures for the British Battalion vary between sources (commonly 375 of about 600, or around 125 left unhurt of 400).

name: Pingarrón hill, Jarama
text: The 695 m Pingarrón dominated the Jarama battlefield and changed hands several times in hand-to-hand fighting. Nationalist troops took it in mid-February; Republican units, including Líster's men and the XV International Brigade, tried repeatedly to retake it. On 27 February the Abraham Lincoln Battalion, about 450 Americans under Robert Merriman, was ordered to attack without the promised artillery and air support and lost well over half its men, among them the Irish poet Charles Donnelly. The Nationalists kept the hill; the battle ended in stalemate, with both armies dug in facing each other until 1939.
look: Ridge-top trenches, stone parapets and nearby Republican positions (Cota 700, Cota 666) with views over the Jarama valley.
plan: Reached on foot by Morata's battle routes 5 and 6 (several km on farm tracks); the town runs occasional guided walks. Rough ground: wear boots.
town: San Martín de la Vega / Morata de Tajuña
disputed: Lincoln Battalion losses on 27 Feb are given variously (e.g. 120 dead and 175 wounded).

name: Valle de Cuelgamuros (former Valle de los Caídos)
text: Franco ordered this basilica cut into the granite of the Guadarrama, crowned by a 150 m cross, as a monument to his victory. Work lasted from 1940 to 1959; the workforce included political prisoners who redeemed sentence by labour. Remains of tens of thousands of dead from both sides were brought here, many Republicans moved from mass graves without their families' consent. Franco himself was buried here in 1975 and exhumed in 2019; José Antonio Primo de Rivera was removed in 2023. The 2022 Democratic Memory Law restored the name Cuelgamuros and plans its re-signification; forensic exhumations in the crypts continue.
look: The monumental esplanade, the rock-cut basilica, the cross (funicular often closed) and the Benedictine abbey behind.
plan: Paid entry; closed Mondays. Access by car via the M-600 from El Escorial; allow half a day with El Escorial. Dress respectfully: it is an active church.
disputed: Numbers vary: around 33,800 people are recorded as interred; how many prisoners worked on the building is disputed (official records of a few hundred convicts at a time, against estimates of up to 20,000 over the whole project).

name: Paracuellos de Jarama cemetery
text: As Nationalist troops reached Madrid in November 1936, thousands of prisoners — officers, priests, Falangists, conservatives — were taken from the Modelo, San Antón, Porlier and Ventas prisons in 'sacas' and shot beside the Arroyo de San José at Paracuellos and at Soto de Aldovea near Torrejón. It was the largest single massacre in the Republican zone. The orders for the removals came from Madrid's public-order authorities under the Junta de Defensa; the degree of responsibility of its councillor Santiago Carrillo, and the role of Soviet advisers, remain contested. The cemetery holds the mass graves and a monument erected after the war.
look: A walled cemetery on the slope with long rows of mass graves, crosses and memorial plaques listing identified victims.
plan: Managed by a private brotherhood; opening is restricted, typically mornings and on commemorative dates. Check locally before going; be respectful.
disputed: Death toll: modern historians mostly give 2,000–3,000 (Thomas c.2,000; Casanova c.2,700), against older claims up to 12,000. Carrillo's personal responsibility is the subject of continuing debate.

name: Telefónica building, Gran Vía
text: Madrid's first skyscraper (1929) was the tallest building in the city and the Republic's eye over the front: from its upper floors observers watched Nationalist movements in the Casa de Campo. It housed the telephone exchange and the Foreign Press Office, where correspondents such as Hemingway and Dos Passos filed censored reports. That made it a target: Nationalist guns on the Garabitas hill hit it again and again (over 120 impacts in October 1936 alone, according to the company's history), but the exchange never stopped working. The stretch of Gran Vía outside became known as 'Shell Alley'.
look: The restored tower dominates Gran Vía; the Espacio Fundación Telefónica inside hosts free exhibitions.
plan: Espacio Fundación Telefónica (entrance on Calle Fuencarral) is free, Tuesday–Sunday. Metro Gran Vía.

name: Museo Reina Sofía — Picasso's Guernica
text: Picasso painted Guernica for the Spanish Republic's pavilion at the 1937 Paris International Exhibition, in response to the bombing of the Basque town by the Condor Legion and Italian aircraft on 26 April 1937. The painting toured to raise support for the Republic and then stayed in New York, as Picasso wished, until democracy returned to Spain; it arrived in Madrid in 1981 and moved to the Reina Sofía in 1992. The surrounding rooms place it among posters, photographs and film from the war, making this the best single introduction in Madrid to the war's propaganda and art.
look: Guernica and its preparatory sketches, with rooms of Civil War posters, photographs and the 1937 pavilion material.
plan: Closed Tuesdays; free entry in the evening on most weekdays (check hours). Photos of Guernica are not allowed. Metro Atocha.

name: Cerro Garabitas, Casa de Campo
text: At 677 m, Garabitas is one of the highest points of the Casa de Campo, the former royal hunting estate through which Nationalist columns attacked Madrid in November 1936. Varela's troops took the hill on 13 November and held it for the rest of the war despite Republican counter-attacks, including by the XI International Brigade. From December 1936 their batteries here shelled the city centre, the Gran Vía and the Telefónica building. The front line across the park stayed almost static until March 1939, and several concrete bunkers from both sides still survive in the woods.
look: A panoramic summit with a ranger watchtower and views over Madrid; scattered bunkers and trench traces in the surrounding park.
plan: Free, open park; walk up from the Lago or Batán Metro stations (about 45 minutes). Take a map: signage for war remains is limited.

name: Parque del Oeste bunkers
text: The northern end of the Parque del Oeste lay right on the front line facing the Nationalist salient in the University City. Nationalist sappers built concrete machine-gun posts here under fire; the stages of construction are still visible in the concrete, and one carries the inscription 'Zapadores nº 7'. Of around twenty such posts, three survive, protected as heritage. They are among the few tangible traces of the two-and-a-half-year siege line inside the city itself.
look: Three sealed concrete machine-gun bunkers among the park's trees and lawns.
plan: Free, open park; 10 minutes' walk from Metro Moncloa. Combine with the University City and Casa de Velázquez.

name: Puente de los Franceses
text: This 19th-century railway bridge over the Manzanares was one of the crossings the Nationalists needed to break into Madrid from the Casa de Campo in November 1936. Republican militias and troops, soon joined by the newly arrived International Brigades, defended it; the fighting here is remembered as part of the Brigades' baptism of fire. It gave its name to a popular Republican song ('Puente de los Franceses, mamita mía, nadie te pasa'). The Nationalists eventually crossed the river further north and entered the University City instead.
look: The original brick-and-granite five-arch bridge, still carrying trains.
plan: View from the Madrid Río riverside path or the Paseo de la Florida; 15 minutes' walk from Príncipe Pío.

name: Templo de Debod — site of the Cuartel de la Montaña
text: Here stood the Montaña barracks, where General Joaquín Fanjul rose for the coup in Madrid on 19 July 1936 and then found himself besieged. On 20 July, armed workers, Assault Guards and loyal troops attacked with artillery and aircraft and stormed it; many of the officers and soldiers inside were killed after the surrender, and Fanjul was later tried and shot. The fall of the barracks secured Madrid for the Republic. The ruined building was demolished after the war, and the Egyptian Temple of Debod was re-erected on the site in 1972.
look: A park with the Egyptian temple; there is no trace of the barracks, but the viewpoint looks towards the Casa de Campo front.
plan: Free park, a short walk from Plaza de España. Best at sunset.
disputed: The number of defenders killed after the surrender is uncertain; accounts range from dozens to several hundred.

name: Posición Jaca bunker, El Capricho park
text: Under the 18th-century garden of the Dukes of Osuna, Republican engineers dug 'Posición Jaca', the command bunker of General Miaja's Army of the Centre and his chief of staff Vicente Rojo, completed in August 1937. Some 15 m underground, it has a central gallery with rooms for about 200 people, generators, ventilation and gas-proof doors. It is one of the best-preserved Civil War command posts in Spain and shows how the defence of Madrid was run once the front had stabilised.
look: The restored underground galleries beneath the romantic garden of El Capricho.
plan: Guided visits only, usually on weekends and by prior booking with the City of Madrid. The park is open weekends and holidays. Metro El Capricho.

name: Museo de la Batalla del Jarama, Morata
text: A small private museum, built up by local enthusiasts, gathers thousands of objects recovered from the Jarama battlefield or donated by veterans and their families: rifles, grenades, pierced helmets, mortars, lamps from the refuge caves, coins, passes and ration cards. It is the natural starting point for the battlefield, which saw Nationalist forces under Varela cross the Jarama in February 1937 and Republican troops, with the International Brigades, stop them short of the Madrid–Valencia road at a cost of many thousands of casualties on each side.
look: Display rooms of battlefield finds, maps and photographs.
plan: Located in the Mesón El Cid, Calle Carmen, Morata de Tajuña (tel. 918 730 181); ask there for opening. Morata hosts a battle re-enactment each February.

name: International Brigades memorials, Jarama
text: Along the Morata–San Martín de la Vega road, near the XV Brigade's old kitchens at the Venta de Frascuelo, stand memorials to the British, Irish, American, Balkan and Franco-Belgian volunteers who fought on the Jarama. Nearby on the Casas Altas hill a sculpture by Martín Chirino of two clasped hands honours all who fought in the battle. For decades after 1939 the Brigades could not be commemorated in Spain; these memorials were raised by associations and veterans' families after the return of democracy.
look: Memorial stones and plaques by the road, and the Chirino sculpture among trenches and refuge caves.
plan: On Morata's battle route 4; roadside parking. Combine with Suicide Hill (1.5 km) and Pingarrón.

name: Brunete
text: On 6 July 1937 the Republic launched its first great offensive west of Madrid, aiming to cut off the Nationalist troops besieging the capital and to relieve pressure on the northern front. Líster's 11th Division took Brunete by surprise on the first day, but the attack stalled on Nationalist strongpoints at Villanueva de la Cañada and Quijorna and in the July heat. From 18 July Varela's counter-offensive, backed by the Condor Legion, pushed back, and Brunete was retaken on 24 July. The village was flattened and rebuilt after the war by the Regiones Devastadas agency.
look: A post-war rebuilt town; the parish church on the Plaza Mayor still shows bullet and shrapnel impacts, and the cemetery marks the last phase of fighting.
plan: Free; park near the Plaza Mayor. Combine with Quijorna and Villanueva de la Cañada (15 minutes' drive).
disputed: Republican losses are given as anything from 10,000 to 25,000 killed and wounded; Nationalist losses about 7,000–17,000 depending on source.

name: Brihuega & Palacio de Ibarra
text: In March 1937 Mussolini's Corpo Truppe Volontarie under General Roatta drove down the Zaragoza road towards Guadalajara to encircle Madrid from the north-east. Rain grounded its aircraft on muddy airfields while Republican planes flew from paved runways. At the Palacio de Ibarra, a country house south of Brihuega, the Italian anti-fascist Garibaldi Battalion of the XII International Brigade fought Italian Blackshirts on 13–14 March: Italians against Italians. On 18 March Republican divisions under Líster, Mera and others counter-attacked and retook Brihuega, routing the CTV. It was the Republic's most celebrated victory and a humiliation for Fascist Italy.
look: Brihuega's walled old town above the Tajuña; the ruins of the Palacio de Ibarra stand in fields a few km south-east (private land).
plan: View the Palacio de Ibarra from the track only. Trijueque and Torija, on the N-II, were also battle sites and lie 15–20 minutes away.
disputed: Italian losses are variously given as 600–3,000 dead and 2,000–4,000 wounded; the Republic's propaganda magnified the victory.

name: Frente del Agua, Paredes de Buitrago
text: In late July 1936 rebel troops under Colonel García Escámez crossed the Somosierra and seized Paredes de Buitrago, close to the El Villar and Puentes Viejas reservoirs that supplied Madrid with water. Republican forces, helped by workers of the Canal de Isabel II who fortified the positions, stopped them just short. The front stabilised by the end of August and stayed here for the rest of the war, the Nationalist 72nd Division facing Republican mixed brigades across the valley. The Comunidad de Madrid has cleared and signposted 26 positions of both armies.
look: Trenches, machine-gun nests, shelters and command posts at Loma Quemada (Republican), El Pinar and Peñas Bajas (Nationalist), with information panels.
plan: An 8 km circular waymarked route starts from the interpretation centre in the old village laundry. Allow 3 hours; good footwear.

name: Alto del León (south side), Guadarrama
text: The Guadarrama pass, renamed Alto de los Leones by the victors, was one of the first battlefields of the war. Columns sent by General Mola from Valladolid and Segovia seized it on 22 July 1936 and held it against militia columns from Madrid in bloody fighting over the following days. The front then settled along the crest. Nationalist positions pushed south of the pass towards La Jarosa, the most advanced in the central sector, while Republican lines faced them on the lower slopes. Both sides fortified the mountain with concrete bunkers, shelters and observation posts that survive in the pine woods.
look: A bunker behind the roadside restaurant at the pass, an armoured observation post, and trenches, nests and a vaulted command bunker in the woods towards the La Jarosa reservoir.
plan: A 13 km circular walk links the positions (about 600 m of climbing). Mountain weather: carry warm clothing even in summer. The north side of the pass is in Segovia (see Castile).

name: Cementerio Civil & Almudena execution wall
text: After Madrid fell in March 1939, the eastern wall of the Cementerio del Este (Almudena) became the main place of execution for the city: according to research by historians, close to 3,000 people were shot there between 1939 and 1944, among them the 'Trece Rosas', thirteen young women executed on 5 August 1939. The adjoining Cementerio Civil, for those buried outside the Catholic Church, holds the graves of Republican leaders such as Francisco Largo Caballero, Dolores Ibárruri 'Pasionaria' and Pablo Iglesias, and plaques to the Trece Rosas.
look: Graves and memorials in the Cementerio Civil; the wall of the Almudena cemetery, with a memorial to the victims.
plan: Free; cemetery hours daily. Enter the Cementerio Civil from Calle Carmen Martín Gaite; Metro La Elipa.
disputed: The memorial with the names of the executed commissioned in 2018 was altered by the city council in 2019 after disputes over errors in the lists; the number of those executed (c. 2,900–3,000) is based on cemetery records.

name: Jarama bridges: Pindoque & Arganda
text: The Nationalist offensive of February 1937 needed to cross the Jarama. On the night of 11 February, Moroccan Regulares crept up to the Pindoque railway bridge near Vaciamadrid and silently killed the International Brigade sentries; a Republican attempt to blow the bridge failed, and it survived the explosion. Further south, Barrón's cavalry seized the Arganda road bridge. These crossings opened the way to the hills of Pingarrón and Suicide Hill. Nearby, on the Cerro del Melero at Rivas, stretches of Republican trenches from 1938 have been restored.
look: The railway bridge (rebuilt) and old Arganda road bridge over the Jarama in the Parque Regional del Sureste; restored trenches on the Cerro del Melero.
plan: Reach on foot or by bike from the Laguna del Campillo (Rivas-Vaciamadrid) along the river paths; free.

name: Quijorna
text: Quijorna was one of the Nationalist strongpoints that blunted the Republic's Brunete offensive. Its small garrison held out for three days against Republican divisions before falling on 9 July 1937, costing the attackers time they could not afford. The surrounding hills were then fortified by both sides. Around the village survive a hilltop bunker and, some 2 km behind the Republican line of Cota 640 and Loma Quemada, the camp of La Peña, while the farmhouse of Casa de los Llanos served as a Republican planning centre.
look: A concrete bunker on the hill above the village and remains of the Republican rear camp at La Peña.
plan: Free; walk up from the village. Combine with Brunete and Villanueva de la Cañada.

name: Villanueva de la Cañada & Mosquito Ridge
text: Villanueva de la Cañada, held by a small Nationalist garrison, resisted the Republican offensive through the first day at Brunete and fell only on the night of 7 July, after the XV International Brigade and other units had been pinned in the open wheatfields. North-east of the village, the Republican drive towards Boadilla stalled on the Mosquito Ridge (Loma de los Mosquitos), where the British and American battalions suffered heavily in repeated attacks under a scorching sun. The failure to take the ridge ended hopes of cutting the Nationalist lines west of Madrid.
look: A modern town; the ridge line and open country of the battle are visible from the Villanueva del Pardillo–Boadilla area, with scattered fortifications.
plan: Best seen by car from the M-600 and M-503 roads; no dedicated interpretation on site.

name: Blockhaus 13, Colmenar del Arroyo
text: After the Battle of Brunete the western front of Madrid settled along the Perales valley. In late 1938 the Nationalist 71st Division began a line of large concrete blockhouses here; Blockhaus 13, built by the 2nd Company of the 7th Sapper Battalion, was the only one completed. Designed to withstand heavy artillery and aerial bombs, it has four domed machine-gun nests linked by a central corridor, an inner courtyard and a cistern. Unusually well preserved, it was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 2019.
look: A near-intact reinforced-concrete blockhouse with four circular firing nests.
plan: Signposted near the M-510 between Navalagamella and Colmenar del Arroyo; short walk from the road; free.

name: Sigüenza Cathedral
text: In the autumn of 1936 Nationalist columns advancing from Aragon and Soria besieged Sigüenza. The last Republican militiamen, with civilians, took refuge in the cathedral and held out for several days under artillery and air bombardment before surrendering in mid-October. The cathedral suffered heavy damage: roofs and the crossing collapsed, sculpture was shattered and the 18th-century organ destroyed. It was restored in the 1940s, when a new lantern tower was added over the crossing.
look: The fortress-like Romanesque–Gothic cathedral, restored; post-war repairs and the new lantern are visible.
plan: Cathedral open daily with a paid guided route for the museum and sacristy; Sigüenza is 1 h 45 min from Madrid by train.

name: Cerro de los Ángeles
text: The hill at Getafe, near Spain's geographic centre, carried the monument to the Sacred Heart of Jesus consecrated by Alfonso XIII in 1919. In the anticlerical violence of summer 1936, militiamen staged a mock 'execution' of the statue by firing squad, photographed for the press, and the monument was dynamited on 7 August. In November the Nationalists took the hill and it remained close to the front for the rest of the war. Franco's regime rebuilt a larger monument (1944–1965), a symbol of the 'crusade' narrative.
look: The rebuilt monument and basilica; ruins of the original monument and bullet marks on the monument and convent walls.
plan: Free; open daily. Drive or bus from Getafe; views over southern Madrid.

name: Arco de la Victoria (Moncloa)
text: This 40 m triumphal arch at the entrance to the University City was built in 1950–56 to commemorate the Francoist victory in the battle for the University City, where the front ran from November 1936 to March 1939. Its Latin inscriptions praise Franco's army and the rebuilt university. Since the Democratic Memory laws it has been the subject of debate over re-naming and re-signification; the avenue beneath it was renamed Avenida de la Concordia in 2024.
look: The arch itself, seen from the Moncloa interchange; it cannot be entered.
plan: View from outside, beside Metro Moncloa; combine with the University City and the Parque del Oeste.

name: Fresnedillas de la Oliva bunkers
text: Nationalist troops took Fresnedillas de la Oliva on 5 November 1936 during the advance on Madrid; the front then halted on the Perales river and saw heavy fighting in December 1936. In 1937 the Nationalists fortified the heights around the village with machine-gun nests, trenches and catenary-vaulted shelters, forming part of the western front of Madrid. Several of these positions, including those of Cota 960, can be visited along local paths.
look: Concrete machine-gun posts, connecting trenches and vaulted storage shelters around the village.
plan: One bunker is by the M-521 towards Robledo de Chavela; others require short walks. Free.

name: Los Yesares positions, Pinto
text: South of Madrid, between Pinto and Valdemoro, the Nationalist line that ran from the Cerro de los Ángeles to the Jarama was dug into the gypsum hills. At Los Yesares, archaeologists of the Comunidad de Madrid have recorded four concrete-and-masonry posts, trenches, rifle pits and a shelter on a limestone hill. The site shows the static rear lines that followed the Jarama battle. A similar Nationalist position was excavated at El Espartal near Valdemoro.
look: Four small fortins, trenches and a shelter on a low hill.
plan: Accessible on foot from Pinto; little signage, so use a GPS track. Free.

name: Bustarviejo penal labour camp
text: After the war the regime used political prisoners as forced labour on public works under the 'redemption of sentences through work' scheme. At Bustarviejo, prisoners built the Madrid–Burgos railway between 1944 and 1952, living in a camp that has been studied by archaeologists of the CSIC and the Comunidad de Madrid. It is one of the few such camps in Spain whose remains can be seen, and complements Cuelgamuros as evidence of prison labour.
look: Foundations of three compounds, guard posts, a punishment cell and nearby railway cuttings and tunnels.
plan: Signposted path outside the village; free, open access. Allow an hour.
